summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 71) and fuel prices remain high, but the work‑from‑home mandate is delivering only a fraction of its projected fuel savings. Public transport ridership is modestly below pre‑pandemic levels, while high‑mobility, low‑WFH sectors pose economic and environmental risks.

signals.detail: Only 334,000 litres were saved in the first week of the mandate, roughly 1% of the modelled ceiling of 35.7 M L/week, indicating that the policy’s fuel‑saving impact is currently negligible despite a 100‑point fuel policy component.

Daily PT trips total 1.24 M, about 13% below the pre‑pandemic daily average (~1.43 M). The ridership component of the MF‑Index sits at 72.7, suggesting a moderate but not yet critical dip in public‑transport usage.

Retail & Services, Logistics, and Construction show mobility scores of 85‑95 with WFH rates under 15%, flagging high exposure to congestion, fuel cost volatility, and productivity losses in sectors that drive the economy.

While overall WFH adoption is 60%, it is uneven: public & GLCs enjoy 60% WFH, but high‑risk sectors lag at 5‑15%, creating an inequitable distribution of mobility burden and limiting the policy’s overall effectiveness.

Elevated RON95 (RM4.27) and diesel (RM5.12) prices could encourage a shift to mass transit, yet ridership remains below pre‑COVID levels and fuel‑saving outcomes are minimal, indicating only a tentative move toward modal change.

recommendation: Strengthen compliance monitoring for the WFH mandate in high‑mobility sectors, targeting at least 30% WFH in Retail, Logistics and Construction within six months. Pair this with a graduated fuel‑tax rebate for firms that achieve verified reductions in vehicle kilometres. Simultaneously, boost PT incentives (fare discounts, service frequency) to close the 13% ridership gap by end‑2027.
